## Introduction
Looking for the best budget gaming PC build 2026? You’re in the right place. This guide walks you through every part you need to hit solid 1080p performance without breaking the bank. We’ll focus on price‑to‑performance picks that stay relevant for the next couple of years, while keeping the total cost under a reasonable ceiling. Whether you’re a first‑time builder or upgrading an old rig, the steps below will help you assemble a machine that feels modern, runs smoothly, and leaves room for future tweaks.

## Core Parts
A gaming PC hinges on five main components: processor, graphics card, motherboard, memory, and storage. Power supply, case, and cooling round out the build. Choosing each wisely ensures you avoid bottlenecks and keep upgrade paths open. We’ll break down the current 2026 market, highlight the best value options, and explain why they work together.

### CPU Choices
For a budget build, AMD’s Ryzen 5 7600X and Intel’s Core i5‑13400F remain top contenders. The 7600X offers six cores, twelve threads, and strong single‑core speed, perfect for esports titles. The i5‑13400F mixes performance and efficiency cores, delivering solid multitasking at a slightly lower price. Both chips support DDR5 and PCIe 5.0, giving you a foundation for future upgrades. Aim for a price around $150‑$180; any cheaper and you risk losing noticeable frame rates in newer games.

### GPU Options
The graphics card is where most of your budget goes. In 2026, the NVIDIA RTX 4060 and AMD Radeon RX 7600 XT sit at the sweet spot for 1080p high‑settings gaming. The RTX 4060 brings DLSS 3 and ray‑tracing support, while the RX 7600 XT offers comparable raster performance with lower power draw. Expect to spend $260‑$300. If you can stretch a bit, the RTX 4060 Ti adds extra VRAM for texture‑heavy titles, but the base models already deliver 60+ FPS in most modern games at 1080p.

### Motherboard Guide
Pair your CPU with a B650 (AMD) or B760 (Intel) motherboard. These chipsets provide PCIe 5.0 slots for the GPU, DDR5 support, and plenty of USB ports without the premium of X670/Z790 boards. Look for models with solid VRM cooling, at least two M.2 slots, and BIOS flashback for easy updates. Prices typically range from $110‑$150. Brands like MSI, ASUS, and Gigabyte offer reliable options that won’t bottleneck your build.

### Memory & Storage
16 GB of DDR5‑5600 RAM is the sweet spot for gaming in 2026. It balances cost and performance, leaving enough headroom for background apps. Opt for a dual‑channel kit (2×8 GB) to maximize bandwidth. For storage, a 1 TB NVMe SSD (PCIe 4.0) gives fast load times and ample space for a library of games. Brands like Crucial, Western Digital, and Kingston offer reliable drives under $80. If you need more space later, adding a second SSD or a large HDD is straightforward.

### Power & Cooling
A 550‑W 80+ Bronze PSU provides reliable power for this build while keeping costs low. Choose a unit from reputable makers such as Corsair, EVGA, or Seasonic, ensuring it has enough 8‑pin PCIe connectors for your GPU. For cooling, the stock CPU cooler that comes with the Ryzen 5 7600X or Intel i5‑13400F is adequate for non‑overclocked use. If you prefer lower temps or plan to push the CPU, an affordable aftermarket air cooler like the Cooler Master Hyper 212 Evo ($35) works well.
